1:
Hello everyone. My name is Yasir Alyoubi. My principal supervisor is Professor Farookh Hussain, and my co-supervisor is Dr Firas Al-Doghman. Today I present my candidature reassessment.

My research title is A Trusted Authorization Framework for Multi-Party Patient Consent in Healthcare Data Sharing. My research asks one main question. Before any patient data is shared, how can a system check the patient's consent together with identity, authority, approvals, policy and time, all in one decision?
2:
This slide is the outline of my talk. It has eleven parts.

I start with the introduction and the systematic literature review. Then I show the research gaps, the research questions and the research objectives. After that I explain the research methodology and the proposed solutions.

Next, I show the implementation and evaluation of my prototype. I finish with the significance of the research, the research plan and the references.
3:
This slide explains why this research is needed.

First, healthcare data is very sensitive. It is shared between many independent parties, like patients, guardians, doctors and hospitals.

Second, consent is usually kept as a passive record. It only says that permission was given.

Third, identity is not authority. A system may know who you are. That does not mean you may see this patient's data.

Fourth, even with approval, a request can ask for more data, or for another purpose, than the patient allowed.

So the last point is that we need one trusted decision that checks all these conditions together.

The box on the right states the central problem. No current mechanism links all these conditions in one decision and also shows that it is secure. "Formally" means with exact definitions. "Empirically" means with tests and measurements.
4:
This slide defines the key ideas I use in the whole research.

The top row has three questions. Identity asks if we can reliably know who the participant is. For this I use a DID, which means a decentralised identifier. Authority asks if the participant has the right role or permission. For this I use a VC, which means a verifiable credential. Multi-party approval asks if all required guardians approved, and if each one was checked on their own.

In the second row, Policy asks if the request stays inside the allowed purpose, data scope and jurisdiction. Time and lifecycle asks if the consent is still valid, and not expired or revoked.

The dark box brings it together. Consent becomes an object the system can evaluate: C equals I, A, P, T, L, E. That is identity, authority, policy, time, jurisdiction and evidence. Authority holds the guardian set G and the threshold N, which is the number of approvals needed. L means jurisdiction, not lifecycle. Whether the consent is active or revoked is kept in E.
5:
This slide shows how I ran the systematic literature review. I read the table from top to bottom.

Protocol: I followed PRISMA 2020. This is a standard guide that makes a review clear and repeatable. A written protocol, version 1.1, fixed the questions, databases, query, criteria and quality items before screening started.

Search: I used one master query with three concept blocks joined by AND. The blocks cover healthcare data, consent and authorisation, and trust and multi-party ideas. I searched seven databases. Google Scholar was only a discovery arm, so its results are reported separately.

Dates: the main searches were on 24 and 25 August 2026. ACM Digital Library was searched later, on 5 September 2026.

Screening went from title, to abstract, to full text, with seven inclusion and nine exclusion criteria. For quality, a study is included when QA1 to QA4 add up to at least 3.0.

Possible question: Why was ACM searched later? My UTS Library account was put on hold after I downloaded many full-text PDFs, so I had no access. The library removed the hold, but it took time. I used the same string and fields.
6:
This is the PRISMA flow diagram. It shows how the number of papers went down at each step.

The seven databases returned 9,256 records. Google Scholar, on the right, was only a discovery arm, so it is not added to this total.

After removing duplicates, 6,039 records were screened by title. 2,910 were excluded, mostly because they had no authorisation signal or were outside healthcare. That left 3,129 records for the abstract stage. 2,541 abstracts were screened and 741 were excluded. 588 could not be screened, because the export had no abstracts.

Next, 1,800 full texts were sought and sorted into priority tiers A, B and C. At the reporting checkpoint, 64 full texts were assessed. That is all 39 in Tier A and 25 more. 17 were excluded. The other 1,735 are not assessed yet, and that work continues.

The last box shows the 25 primary studies: 23 core studies plus the 2 supporting studies with the highest quality score.

Possible question: Why does the report say 44 studies? The 25 primary and 19 supporting studies make 44. The 3 secondary studies are kept only for background.
7:
This slide gives the quality assessment rules.

QA1 asks if the study is about patient consent, or data access controlled by consent, in healthcare. QA2 asks if it has a real authorisation or access-decision mechanism, not only storage or recording. QA3 asks if it offers a proper framework, model, protocol or architecture. QA4 asks if the method is tested with a proof of concept or an implementation.

These four items decide inclusion. QA5 to QA8 are extra quality items. They were scored for every included study, but they only place a study in an evidence tier: A, B, C or Background. They do not decide inclusion. These evidence tiers are not the same as the priority tiers on the PRISMA slide.

The last row is the rule. Yes scores 1, Partial scores 0.5 and No scores 0. A study is included when QA1 to QA4 add up to at least 3.0 out of 4.
8:
From the literature, I defined six key requirements for trustworthy multi-party consent. Each requirement matches one research question, and later one research objective.

Req 1: consent should be an object the system can evaluate at access time, not only a record.

Req 2: identity and authority are checked in a decentralised way, with DIDs and verifiable credentials. Identity tells us who the person is. Authority tells us what they may do.

Req 3: multi-party authorisation. A set number of independent approvals, called the threshold, must be reached. So no single person can approve alone.

Req 4: policy and context. Even an approved request must stay inside the allowed purpose, data scope and jurisdiction.

Req 5: time and lifecycle. Expired or revoked consent must not work.

Req 6: auditability and security assurance. Every decision keeps evidence that explains why it was made. The security properties are also defined and tested.

This table is the heart of the review. Each row is one of the 25 studies. Each column is one of the six requirements. Req means requirement.

Green Yes means the study fully meets the requirement. Gold Partial means it meets only part of it. Red No means it does not meet it.

12:
This figure sums up the whole review in one picture. Please read it from left to right.

On the left are the six requirements. Each box shows how many of the 25 studies get a full Yes. Consent representation has 12. Identity and authority has 7. Multi-party authorisation has 6. Policy and context has 10. Temporal and lifecycle has 8. Assurance has 9, but only 4 have a formal proof.

All the arrows lead to the yellow box, the conjunction gap. Conjunction means joining conditions with AND. Each requirement is met somewhere, but no study joins Requirements 1 to 5 in one access decision.

The next box is the assurance gap. The few proofs cover only a small part of the decision. The joined conditions are never proved or tested as one decision.

The dark box at the bottom is my answer. Consent becomes an object C that can be checked. R is the request and t is the time. Access is allowed only when all five checks pass: identity, approval, policy, time and jurisdiction. The symbol ∧ means AND.
13:
From the review, I defined six research gaps. There is one gap for each requirement, with the same number.

Gap 1: consent is kept as a record of permission. Where it can be checked, it holds only some conditions, and only one party issues it.

Gap 2: identity tells us who someone is, not what they may do. Only 10 of the 25 studies check authority separately.

Gap 3: multi-party approval is used as a backup path or a registration step. It is not checked at every access.

Gap 4: purpose, data scope and jurisdiction are rarely checked in the same decision as identity, authority and approval. Jurisdiction means the legal region where the consent may be used.

Gap 5: time, lifecycle and revocation are often checked on a credential or at registration, not at each request.

Gap 6: nobody proves or tests the whole decision. Any proof covers only a small part.

Gaps 1 to 5 together form the conjunction gap. Gap 6 is the assurance gap.
14:
These gaps lead to my main research question. Let me read it.

How can a trust-oriented computing framework establish and enforce trustworthy multi-party consent for decentralised healthcare data sharing under identity, authority, and policy constraints?

Two words are the key here. Establish is about creating trust. That means trusted participants, their authority, and a shared consent decision. Enforce is about checking these conditions each time someone asks for healthcare data.

Trust-oriented means my focus is trust, not one technology. Blockchain, decentralised identity and credentials are tools that support the trust model.

Multi-party means one person alone cannot give the approval. A set of chosen participants must each approve.

The last part of the question names the limits on every decision. These are who the person is, what they are allowed to do, and what the policy permits.
15:
I split the main question into six sub-questions. Each one matches the gap with the same number.

RQ1 asks how to model consent as an object that holds identity, authority, policy and evidence.

RQ2 asks how DIDs and VCs can give us trusted participants. A DID is a decentralised identifier. It does not depend on one central identity provider. A VC is a verifiable credential, for example proof of a role. The key point is to keep proof of identity separate from authority.

RQ3 asks how verified participants can approve together, so no single person can approve alone.

RQ4 asks how purpose and data scope can stop a valid user from reaching data they should not see.

RQ5 asks how to reject access after expiry, revocation or a wrong state change.

RQ6 asks how to define the security properties formally and test them in practice.

RQ1 to RQ5 build the decision. RQ6 checks it.
16:
From the questions, I set six research objectives. Each objective answers the question with the same number. The table shows each one and its status.

RO1 is the consent model. Consent becomes a structured object that can be checked. It is done.

RO2 checks identity and authority with DIDs and VCs, and keeps them apart. It is done.

RO3 is multi-party approval. Each guardian signs with EIP-712, a standard for signing typed data. In the prototype, every listed guardian must sign. It is done.

RO4 checks purpose and data scope. It is done.

So RO1 to RO4 are delivered and validated with the prototype.

RO5, time and lifecycle, is in progress. The validity window and revocation already work. Next I will extend them to consent changes, delegation and guardian-set changes.

RO6 is partially completed. The tests and first measurements are done. The formal analysis comes in the next stage.
17:
This slide shows my research method as seven steps, from left to right.

Step 1 is the problem. Consent is a passive record, and there is no integrated trusted decision.

Step 2 is the systematic literature review. I followed PRISMA 2020, a standard guide for reporting reviews, and analysed 25 primary studies.

Step 3 gives the six gaps and the six research questions. Step 4 sets the six objectives.

Step 5 is the design. It has the MVC architecture, the consent object C and four algorithms.

Step 6 is the prototype, called HALAH. That stands for History Access Link for Authorised Healthcare. Its smart contract, ConsentSBTv3, runs on Sepolia, an Ethereum test network.

Step 7 is the evaluation. I used live scenarios, measurements and twelve attack scenarios. The formal assurance comes in the next stage.

The arrow at the bottom shows the whole path, from the problem to the evaluated prototype.
18:
This figure shows my research architecture. It uses MVC, which means Model, View and Controller. Please read it from top to bottom.

At the top are the four user groups: patients, guardians, healthcare professionals and auditors. Each group has its own interface in the View layer. The View only sends requests. It never decides access.

Every request enters the Controller layer through request validation. The security checks happen here. Identity Verification checks the DID. Authority Verification checks evidence of authority for the case. Approval Aggregation counts the valid approvals from the guardian set G against the threshold N. Policy Enforcement checks purpose and scope. The Decision Engine joins all five checks. Audit Coordination records evidence for every decision.

At the bottom, the Model layer stores the state. This includes identity records, credentials, the consent object C, approvals, policy, evidence and lifecycle state.

The protected healthcare data sit outside all three layers. The Controller releases them only on ALLOW.

Possible question: Does the prototype do full DID resolution now? No. It checks the DID format. Full DID resolution and VC checks are planned for the next stage.
19:
This slide shows the core of my solution in one rule. The box at the top is the decision equation. It says the decision for consent C, request R, at time t is ALLOW only if all five checks are true. The small 'and' symbols mean every check must pass. The double arrow means 'if and only if'.

The five boxes explain each check. VI checks identity and authority. VA checks that all guardians approved, that the token exists and that the consent is not revoked. VP checks the purpose and the data scope. VT checks that the request is inside the validity window. VL checks that the jurisdiction matches.

The points below are simple. If any one check fails, the answer is DENY. In the prototype, a Groth16 zero-knowledge proof must also verify before any data is released. This kind of proof shows something is true without showing the secret behind it. Every decision on an ACTIVE consent is written to the audit ledger with its decision matrix. The matrix shows the result of each check, so an auditor can see why a request was allowed or denied.
20:
Now I go through each research objective. RO1 is the trust-centric consent model, and its status is Done.

The points on the left follow the steps. The patient selects the patient DID, the doctor, the guardians, the data scope, the validity time and the jurisdiction. In the current interface the purpose is fixed to Treatment. The system then checks the input. For example, an empty data scope or a badly formed guardian DID is rejected.

If the input is valid, the system makes a consent identifier and builds the consent object C. C has six parts: identity, authority, policy and data scope, time, jurisdiction and evidence. The consent is saved in the state PENDING_SIGNATURE. Nothing goes on-chain until all guardians approve. Last, the creation is recorded in the audit ledger.

The flowchart on the right shows the same steps from top to bottom. If the input is not valid, the No branch rejects the consent request.
21:
RO2 is about decentralised identity and authority. The status is Done.

A DID is a decentralised identifier. It tells us who the person is. A verifiable credential, or VC, tells us what the person is allowed to do. So identity is not authority. A valid DID alone never gives access.

The formula says VI for user u is true only when the DID is valid, the credential is valid and the person has authority for this consent C.

The flowchart on the right is the target design. It resolves the DID, checks the credential, reads the role claims and compares them with the consent. Every No leads to Reject Participant. If all checks pass, the evidence is recorded.

In the prototype today, I check the DID format and recover each guardian's EIP-712 signature. EIP-712 is a typed signature format on Ethereum, so we can see who signed. Full DID resolution and VC validation are planned for the next stage.
22:
RO3 is about multi-party authorisation. The status is Done. The idea is that no single person can approve alone.

The guardian set G is fixed when the consent is created. Each guardian signs an EIP-712 approval. The system recovers the signer from the signature and checks it. An approval from someone outside G is not counted. A replayed or duplicate approval is not counted either.

The rule is N-of-N. This means every listed guardian must give a valid signature. In the demo there are two guardians, so it is 2-of-2. One approval is not enough.

The flowchart shows this loop. Each valid approval updates the count. If the threshold is not met, the consent stays pending. When it is met, a local token identifier is recorded. The consent becomes active once its start time is reached. The mint is anchored on the Sepolia test network in the background, so it does not delay the guardians or the doctor.
23:
RO4 is about policy and context. The status is Done. A valid identity and full approval are still not enough.

First, the requested scope, SR, must be a non-empty subset of the authorised scope, SC. In simple words, the doctor must ask for something, and only for data the patient allowed. Second, the purpose must be a supported healthcare purpose of the consent. Time and jurisdiction are checked in the same decision.

Then a Groth16 proof must verify before any data is retrieved. This proof shows the consent has not expired, without showing the secret behind it. If it fails, the answer is DENY.

The example makes it clear. The consent allows only Observation and Medication, so a request that adds Procedure is denied.

The flowchart follows the doctor's request from the top. A failed identity check, failed policy checks or a failed proof all lead to Deny Access. If the consent is not ACTIVE, the refusal is shown to the doctor but is not written to the ledger.
24:
RO5 is about time and the consent lifecycle. The status is In Progress.

The validity window has two times, notBefore and expiry. They are stored on-chain, and VT checks them at every request. Revocation also works end to end, including an on-chain revoke transaction.

The diagram shows the lifecycle as a state machine with six states. A consent starts in PENDING_SIGNATURE, which is off-chain. PENDING_TOKEN means the threshold is met but there is no token identifier yet. When all guardian signatures are verified, a local token is recorded. Before the start time the consent is NOT_STARTED. Inside the window it is ACTIVE, and only then can access be granted. After expiry it becomes EXPIRED. A consent can also be REVOKED.

The red arrows are anchored as Sepolia transactions, the mint and the revoke. The dashed arrows show revocation before a token exists, which stays off-chain.

The next stage adds a lifecycle transition check, consent modification, delegation, guardian-set changes and a formal lifecycle model.
25:
RO6 is about formal assurance and empirical validation. The status is Partially completed. The slide separates what is done from what comes next.

First, I have 36 automated tests. They include twelve attack scenarios, A1 to A12. These try things like replayed approvals, unauthorised signers, requests outside the allowed scope and use of a revoked consent. Second, I measured the on-chain cost, the confirmation latency and the processing time. Third, a live request from a different jurisdiction was refused. That request was made against a consent anchored on Sepolia.

The next stage covers formal proofs or model checking of the security properties. It also covers a larger evaluation under load.

The flowchart on the right shows the method. I define the properties and the scenarios. Then I run valid and attack scenarios, collect the evidence and compare observed with expected decisions. If the properties hold, I document the evidence and limitations. If one fails, I analyse it and refine the framework.
26:
This slide shows the HALAH prototype. HALAH stands for History Access Link for Authorised Healthcare. Each box is one part of it.

There are four interfaces, for the patient, guardian, doctor and auditor. The smart contract is ConsentSBTv3. It is a soulbound ERC-721 token that follows ERC-5484. Soulbound means it cannot be moved to another account. It runs on the Sepolia test network. Guardian approval uses EIP-712 typed signatures, checked by signature recovery.

The access proof is a Groth16 zero-knowledge proof over a Poseidon commitment. Poseidon is a hash function. The proof shows the consent has not expired, without showing the secret. The data are synthetic Synthea records: Observation, Medication, Condition and Procedure. So no real patient is involved. Last, the audit ledger keeps evidence of every decision, and no medical content goes on-chain.

Possible question: Is anything sensitive on-chain? The plaintext purpose is visible in the mint transaction input. I state this in the report.
27:
This slide shows two real screens from the doctor subsystem of the HALAH prototype. Both use the same evaluated consent, f050c29a.

On the left, the doctor enters the consent ID and declares the requester jurisdiction as AU. The consent was issued for AU. Below that is the decision matrix. VI is identity and authority. VA is collective approval, and revocation is also checked inside VA. VP is policy and context. VT is time. VL is jurisdiction. All five show PASS, so the decision is ALLOW and the consent state is ACTIVE.

On the right, the same doctor asks for the four data modules again. This time the declared jurisdiction is SA, not AU. Every check passes except VL. My rule needs all five checks to be true together, so one failure is enough. The system refuses the request and names VL as the failed check.

Possible question: Why refuse if identity and approval were valid? Valid identity and approval do not mean every request is allowed. Each request is checked against all the conditions.
28:
This slide shows the public evidence on the Sepolia test network.

On the left is the Sepolia Etherscan page for the revoke transaction of token number 1. It was confirmed in block 11,771,307 on 24 September 2026. The status says Success. The input data shows the function revoke with the token ID. Anyone can check this record, so it is not only in my own database.

On the right is the gas used by the five anchored transactions. Gas is the unit of computing work on Ethereum. The first two bars are token 8 from the earlier deployment. The other three are on the current contract, ConsentSBTv3.

A mint creates a token and writes a full consent record, so it costs much more. A revoke changes only one flag. For token 1, the revoke used about one sixth of the gas of its mint.

No fee was higher than 0.00021 ETH. Sepolia ether has no money value, so gas is the fair way to compare cost.
29:
This slide is about validation. Validation asks one simple question: does the system make the right decision? I read the table from top to bottom.

The first row is the valid scenarios. A real, allowed request must get access. A scenario passes only when the observed decision is the same as the expected decision. In scenarios 1 to 3, the consent was created, both guardians approved, and the doctor got ALLOW. These cover RQ1 to RQ4.

The second row is the negative scenarios. A wrong request must be refused. If any one check fails, the answer is DENY. In scenario 4, the doctor declared the jurisdiction SA, so VL failed and the request was refused. In scenario 5, the consent was revoked, so the request failed at VA.

The third row is the twelve attack scenarios, A1 to A12. After the hardening, eleven of them are refused. A11 is different. A rewritten audit event changes its digest, but nothing in the prototype compares the digest yet.

The next slide shows these twelve attacks in detail.

The fourth row is the automated tests. There are 23 functional and regression tests and 13 adversarial tests. All 36 pass.

The last row is independent verification. A separate tool reads the receipts from Sepolia and compares them with the local consent state. The result was: all checks passed.

Possible question: Which objectives does this validate? RO1 to RO4, and the parts of RO5 that already work, the validity window and revocation. This validation is the completed part of RO6. The formal proofs and a larger evaluation are planned for the next stage.
30:
Here I tested the system against attacks. The table lists twelve attack scenarios, A1 to A12. The dots show which part each attack targets. I is identity, A is authority, P is policy and scope, T is time, L is jurisdiction, and E is evidence and revocation. Contract means the ConsentSBTv3 contract, run on an in-memory test machine, not on Sepolia.

Examples are a signer outside the guardian set G, a replayed signature, the same guardian approving twice, a request outside the scope, an expired or revoked consent, and a tampered proof.

The two columns on the right show the result before and after the hardening. Before, three attacks, A1, A3 and A5, were accepted when the service functions were called directly. The interface of the 24 September demonstration already refused them. After the hardening, eleven of the twelve are refused, and all 36 automated tests pass.

A11 is different. A rewritten audit event changes its digest, but no part of the prototype compares the digest yet. So I mark it as neutral, not as a pass.
31:
This slide is about evaluation. Evaluation asks a different question: how much does the system cost, and how fast is it? Each row is one metric, with its definition, its formula and the result I measured.

Gas used is the computing work of each transaction on Sepolia. The mint of token 1 used 196,406 gas. Its revoke used only 32,980, about one sixth, because a revoke changes only one flag.

The transaction fee is gas used times the gas price. No fee was above 0.00021 ETH. Sepolia ETH has no money value, so gas is the fair way to compare cost.

Latency is the time from the local event to the on-chain event. The median was 11.5 seconds, between 4.9 and 22.1 seconds over five transactions. It runs in the background, so the guardians and the doctor do not wait for it.

Processing time is the time of each part of a decision. The decision rule takes about 2 microseconds. One guardian signature takes about 11 milliseconds. The Groth16 proof is the slow part, about 1.4 seconds to generate and 0.47 seconds to verify.

The last row is the on-chain read. Reading the contract on Sepolia takes a little over half a second.

I measured these on 1 October 2026, in one container and with five transactions, so the results are indicative only.

The next slide shows all the processing times in detail.
32:
This slide shows how long each part of the system takes. I measured it on 1 October 2026, in the development container I used for the demonstration. The results come from one container and five transactions, so they are indicative only.

In the table, the median is the middle value. The column n is how many times I measured each step. The symbol µs means microseconds, and ms means milliseconds.

The decision rule with its five checks takes about 2 microseconds, so it costs almost nothing. Recovering one guardian signature takes about 11 milliseconds. The Groth16 proof is the slow part of an access request. It takes about 1.4 seconds to generate and about 0.47 seconds to verify. The two read functions on the Sepolia contract take a little over half a second each.

Anchoring on Sepolia is the slowest step, about 11.5 seconds at the median. But it runs in the background, so the guardians and the doctor do not wait for it. The chart on the right shows the same results on a log scale.

Possible question: Why is the proof so slow? The time includes starting the process, not only the cryptographic work.
33:
This table compares traditional EHR access control with my HALAH framework, row by row. EHR means electronic health record.

Identity: traditional systems depend on a central identity provider. In HALAH, every participant uses a decentralised identifier, or DID, and identity is kept separate from authority.

Consent: traditionally it is a passive record. In HALAH it is an object, C, with six parts, and it is checked at every request.

Approval: traditional permissions are set by one party. In HALAH, all N guardians must sign with EIP-712, so no single party can authorise alone.

Access check: traditionally the system logs the user in and checks a fixed permission. In HALAH, the small wedge symbol means AND. All five checks must be true, and a Groth16 proof must pass before data is released.

Time and revocation: once a permission is stored, these are hard to verify. In HALAH, the validity window and revocation are checked at each request, and a revoke is also a transaction on the chain.

Audit: each decision on an ACTIVE consent is logged with its decision matrix, and the consent state is anchored on Sepolia.
34:
This slide explains how the prototype handles data and privacy. I will go through the table from top to bottom.

Data source: I use no real patient data. The records are synthetic, made from the Synthea dataset. They cover four modules: Observation, Medication, Condition and Procedure.

Data storage: the medical records stay off-chain, inside the application. No medical content is written to the blockchain.

On-chain record: the ConsentSBTv3 token stores only pseudonymous patient and requester addresses, a hash of the purpose, the validity window, a two-letter jurisdiction code and a revocation flag. Pseudonymous means the address does not show a real name.

Access to data: records are released only when the decision is ALLOW, and only inside the authorised scope.

Audit: each decision on an ACTIVE consent is saved in the audit ledger with its decision matrix.

The last row is a limitation I want to be honest about. The plain purpose text is passed in the mint transaction, so anyone can see it in the public transaction input.
35:
Now the scientific significance of the research. There are five boxes.

First, consent as an object. Consent is not just a stored record. It is an object, C, with six parts: identity, authority, policy, time, jurisdiction and evidence. The system evaluates it at each request.

Second, standing multi-party approval. Approval is not a one-time step. It is a condition of every access decision, and the patient decides who must approve.

Third, one integrated decision. Identity is kept separate from authority. Then identity, authority, approval, policy, time and jurisdiction are all checked together.

Fourth, the evidence-based review. My PRISMA 2020 review of 25 primary studies found two gaps. The conjunction gap means no study combines all these conditions in one decision. The assurance gap means these conditions are not proved or tested together as one decision.

Fifth, the validated prototype. The framework runs on Sepolia, and I evaluated it with measurements and twelve attack scenarios.
36:
This second significance slide is about the social side, meaning what the research can do for people.

First, it gives patients and their guardians a direct role in deciding who can see the patient's data.

Second, it stops one person from approving access to sensitive health data alone. All the required guardians must approve.

Third, every access decision can be explained and checked later. This helps auditors and healthcare organisations.

Fourth, the medical records stay off-chain. Only the consent evidence goes on the blockchain.

Finally, these points support trust when health data is shared between hospitals and other independent parties. These parties do not belong to one organisation, so each decision needs evidence that others can check.

Thank you for listening. That is the end of my presentation, and I am happy to answer your questions.

Possible question: Why use blockchain at all? It gives persistence, traceability and evidence of the consent state. The token stores only pseudonymous addresses, a hash of the purpose, the validity window, a jurisdiction code and a revocation flag.

Possible question: What is new in this work? Multi-party approval is a standing condition of every access decision, and the patient defines who must approve. I tested the prototype against twelve attack scenarios. After hardening, eleven of them are refused.

Possible question: What is left for the next stage? RO5, on temporal and lifecycle trust, is in progress. RO6, on formal security assurance and empirical validation, is partially completed.
